title: Pivot Points: finding the fixed facts of you and your company, then building strategy around them
summary: Jason Cohen replaces "strengths/weaknesses" and SWOT thinking with "Pivot Points": non-judgmental facts about a person or company that you build around. He gives prompts to find personal ones, a reverse-engineering workshop for a company's, and nine ways to apply them to strategy, positioning and ICP, plus a rule for when changing one is worth it.

principles.text: Treat traits as non-judgmental Pivot Points, not strengths or weaknesses, because their value depends on context.
principles.quote: Pivot Points are strengths in some situations, hindrances in others, and irrelevant in still others.

principles.text: Build strategy around fixed Pivot Points in the short term; only invest to change one when the upside is enormous.
principles.quote: Change Pivot Points only when the upside is so enormous, that even if you achieve only 30% of the transformation you were hoping for, it was still worthwhile.

principles.text: Ask references for the ideal and the worst-case scenario for a person to surface their real Pivot Points past sanitized praise.
principles.quote: What is the ideal scenario, under which this person thrives?

principles.text: Your biggest edge is what comes so naturally you can't see it; ask others to name it.
principles.quote: Definitionally you can't see them yourself, because you don't realize how special they are. Ask others.

principles.text: Find company Pivot Points by observing behavior and results like an outside consultant, not by asking people why they did things.
principles.quote: You're allowed to observe behaviors and results, but not allowed to interrogate people to understand *why* they took those actions.

principles.text: Pick a strategy that matches the founder's Pivot Points and the market, e.g. a competitive founder attacks a stagnant market with a 10x product.
principles.quote: All of these are wonderful strategies, so long as they match the founder's Pivot Points, and the needs of the chosen market.
